newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss vow to clear up 1949 deal on Polish wealth.
newsitem.headline: Swiss vow to clear up 1949 deal on Polish wealth.

text.p: Switzerland said on Saturday it would dig up more details of a secret 1949 accord ceding Poles' unclaimed wealth in Swiss banks to Warsaw before answering World Jewish Congress (WJC) charges it had robbed Holocaust victims.

The Swiss foreign ministry sparked outrage among Jewish groups on Friday by acknowledging the confidential pact, which was contained in an exchange of letters accompanying a treaty compensating Swiss citizens for nationalised property.

In New York, a vice president of the WJC, Kalman Sultanik, said the admission proved that the Swiss "immorally transferred Jewish assets to Poland". He demanded the Swiss pay millions of dollars in compensation to a Jewish restitutions group.

The Swiss foreign ministry said it would study the case more closely and find more details about what payments had actually been made and then respond to allegations that Switzerland had improperly stripped Holocaust victims of their wealth.
"I am not refuting the accusation of immorality. I am saying it is a little too early to make such a general comment for the time being," ministry spokesman Jean-Philippe Tissieres said.
"We won't escape our past. We want to dig into it now and the facts will come very soon," he added, saying he expected more details to emerge before the end of the year.
The 1949 bilateral treaty publicly called for Poland to pay Switzerland 52.1 million Swiss francs ($41 million at 1996 rates) for property the then-communist regime had seized.
The unpublished accompanying letters agree that Polish citizens' Swiss bank accounts and life insurance policies that went unclaimed for five years would be turned over to Poland.
The Swiss foreign ministry has adamantly denied that the deal let Switzerland keep Holocaust victims' riches for itself, as U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato and other critics have suggested.

"Various sides alleged yesterday that Switzerland struck a secret accord with Poland after World War Two that let Switzerland seize for itself dormant assets of Polish citizens. This allegation is wrong," the ministry said on Friday.

Switzerland also struck post-war compensation accords with Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Romania and Hungary, it said. It was still checking whether they contained similar provisions on assets seizures and whether they were enacted.

The Swiss Bankers Association also said on Friday it had discovered a 1950 memo it circulated drawing banks' attention to the 1949 exchange of letters and asking how much money was at stake. It did not give a figure.

The Swiss foreign minister told his cabinet colleagues on March 22, 1950 that not much money would be transferred to Poland under the accord, according to a summary of the meeting found in an U.S. Jewish group's archives.

"The total of these Polish assets in Switzerland is probably less than in general assumed," he is quoted as saying. "There are estimations of two millions (francs). One cannot say whether this figure corresponds to the facts."

Swiss banks have never disputed they were a popular refuge for the wealth of European Jews fearing Nazi persecution after Hitler came to power in Germany in 1933. Many were drawn by Switzerland's strict bank secrecy and neutral status.

But the banks reject WJC claims that they may be sitting on billions of dollars in assets left behind by Jewish account holders murdered in the Holocaust without having passed along their secret bank details.
